title: 2015 annual traffic count: PTH 12 at Loewen Blvd flagged as the signalized intersection most in need
themes: traffic-study; pth12; pth52; intersection; signals; pedestrian
summary: The city manager presented the city's 18th annual traffic count (MMM Group) covering intersections on PTH 12 and PTH 52. Traffic was growing about 2.5% a year; PTH 12 at Penfeld/Acres was the unsignalized intersection most in need (signals scheduled for 2016), PTH 12 at Loewen Boulevard the signalized one most in need, and no crossing met the pedestrian-corridor warrant. A request from Steinbach Christian High School for a pedestrian corridor near Millwork Drive/Stonebridge Crossing was still pending with Manitoba Infrastructure.
status_detail: Report received; the recording ends (9:55) during council questions, so the vote on receiving it is not on video. The Penfeld/Acres signals were built in 2016 (see 2016-pth12-penfeld-acres-intersection); Loewen/PTH 12 was still flagged a year later.
figures: Average traffic growth about 2.5% a year; 18th annual count, first done 1997 (transcript 0:04:00).
reasons: engineering-warrant: Pedestrian counts did not meet the warrant for a formal pedestrian corridor on PTH 12 or PTH 52, including near the Christian high school. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: Steinbach Christian High School (organization) had a pending request with Manitoba Infrastructure for a pedestrian corridor near its school on PTH 12.
notes: Video for Jan 5, 2016 is only 9:55 long and ends mid-question.

title: Old Tom Road (boundary road) paved in full despite a $200,000 overrun
summary: The 2016 plan set $1M to asphalt Old Tom Road, part of the boundary (periphery) roads program. A resident letter asked for a sidewalk too; council kept that for its sidewalk program. The low tender (Bituminex, $1,058,417) put the project about $200,000 over budget; on Apr 5 council tabled it (Siemens) and on May 3 approved the full tender (Zwaagstra), with the extra from surplus or the capital development reserve. Residents also raised speeding; staff had done a traffic count in fall 2015 and were reviewing traffic control.
status_detail: Full tender awarded May 3, 2016 and the road was paved in 2016. In Jan 2017 a councillor described Industrial Road and Old Tom Road as 'unofficial bypasses' around the city. No traffic-control recommendation for Old Tom was found later in the period.
figures: Budget $1M; low tender $1,058,417 plus ~$140,000 engineering, ~$200,000 over (2016-04-05 part 2, 0:23:44); a sidewalk estimated at $700,000–$800,000 (2016-02-02, 1:19:50); capital development reserve ~$500,000 after the draw (2016-05-03, 0:04:37).
reasons: cost: Over budget, information arrived the same day; table to find funds rather than cut scope. (Jac Siemens); cost: A sidewalk would be a separate decision; tying sidewalks to paving would slow boundary-road paving. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: A Lyons Gate couple (Mr. and Mrs. T.) wrote asking for a sidewalk with the paving (Feb 2016); a Clearspring Green resident wrote about speeding on Old Tom Road (May 2016).
decision_source: transcript 2016-05-03 (tabling 2016-04-05: moved Siemens, seconded Fehr, passed)
notes: Old Tom Road is a boundary road, not a highway; included because it was later described as a bypass route that takes traffic off PTH 12.

title: PTH 12 at Penfeld/Acres Drive rebuilt with signals and turn lanes (final year of 3-year PTH 12 program)
summary: Council awarded the 2016 PTH 12 improvement tender (Penfeld/Acres Drive intersection: signals, turn lanes) to Highway Construction Inc. for $2,232,578.50, the last year of a three-year PTH 12 program cost-shared 50/50 with the province under the Urban Highway Fund (earlier phases: Park Road, Stonebridge/Millwork, down to Madison). Work ran through fall 2016; in Dec 2017 council authorized $571,150.40 of extra work that the province had approved and paid for 100%.
status_detail: Intersection open and 'functioning well' by Nov 15, 2016. Dec 19, 2017: council approved the province-funded overrun (moved Zwaagstra, seconded Fehr, carried); total project just over $3.6M, city share about $1.25M (about one third instead of half).
figures: Tender $2,232,578.50 vs engineer's estimate $2,781,000; budget $2.5M, expected total ~$2.47M; 50/50 cost share, city half from capital development reserve (2016-04-05 transcript 0:03:36–0:05:28). 2016 financial plan: $6.6M new capital incl. PTH-12 intersection work, final year of a 3-year program (2016-02-16 hearing 0:01:21). Extra province-paid work $571,150.40; total just over $3.6M, city ~$1.25M (2017-12-19 transcript 0:04:37, 0:06:03).
public: Mayor thanked PTH 12 businesses (e.g. Highway Mazda, named business) for their patience during construction.
decision_source: transcript 2016-04-05; 2017-12-19 overrun moved by Zwaagstra, seconded by Fehr, carried
notes: Which Councillor Penner seconded on 2016-04-05 is not stated in the transcript.

title: Traffic kept as one of council's four RCMP policing priorities; traffic charges up
summary: Each year council set the Steinbach RCMP detachment's performance priorities: police visibility, organized crime/drugs, property crime and traffic. In Apr 2016 the staff sergeant reported that RCMP traffic services were much reduced in the area and that he had asked for more patrols; by Sep 2017 traffic charges were up about 100 for the first half of the year and he linked this to fewer collisions.
status_detail: Priorities confirmed Apr 5, 2016 (moved Funk, seconded Zwaagstra) and Sep 19, 2017 (moved Funk, seconded Zwaagstra), both carried.
figures: Traffic charges Jan–Jun: 237 (2016) vs 323 (2017); impaired charges 41 → 23 (2017-09-19, 0:00:51). Steinbach–Blumenort traffic ~13,000 vehicles/day (2016-04-05 part 2, 0:18:08).
reasons: police-decide: Council sets priorities; enforcement is RCMP work, aided by MPI-funded overtime. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: RCMP Staff Sergeant H.L. (detachment commander) reported reduced RCMP traffic services in 2016 and higher enforcement in 2017.
notes: The RCMP officer is a public official, not a resident, but is given by initials here to be safe.

title: Park Road West carrying detour traffic: who pays to upgrade a peripheral road?
summary: A Councillor Penner noted heavy traffic on gravel Park Road West during PTH 12 construction and asked, under council's priority of 'traffic planning for the future', whether it would be surfaced as a peripheral road. The city manager said road upgrades are developer-driven and the right design (planned as 4 lanes) was undecided; the mayor said the city's own share would be considered with the periphery road program and 'traffic management ideas'.
status_detail: No decision in the period; a Dec 2017 variance hearing still described Park Road West as gravel toward PTH 12.
figures: Planned profile 4 lanes where fronting land is developed (transcript 0:14:51).
reasons: development-first: Road improvements are developer-driven; only one side of the road is developed, which complicates funding. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); study-first: To be answered as the periphery road program and traffic management ideas are reviewed. (Chris Goertzen)

title: Siemens asks that all four PTH 12 lanes stay open during Summer in the City construction
summary: With PTH 12 construction under way, Councillor Siemens asked whether the contractors could keep four lanes open for the Summer in the City weekend, noting the highway was cut to two lanes during the 2015 festival. The city manager said he would make the request.
status_detail: Staff agreed to pass on the request; no report back found in later 2016 transcripts.
reasons: provincial-highway: Depends on the contractor's construction schedule and lane changes already made. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))

title: Peak-hour no-parking on Main Street East after the speed limit rose to 60 km/h
summary: After the Highway Traffic Board raised the speed on part of Main Street East from 50 to 60 km/h (2015), staff recommended no parking 7–9 a.m. and 3–6 p.m., Monday–Saturday, from east of Kroeker Avenue to mid-block between Goossen and McKenzie. Siemens wanted no parking at all there and moved an amendment to start the restriction at Goossen; it was defeated and the staff recommendation carried. Siemens noted council had earlier asked the province to cut the speed east of the city to 50 km/h and was refused.
status_detail: Peak-hour restrictions approved; the mayor said their value depends on enforcement and suggested reviewing them in a year (no review found in the period).
figures: Speed zone 50 → 60 km/h (HTB, 2015); a traffic study found most cars at 55–60 km/h in the posted 50 zone (transcript 0:03:56, 0:12:39).
reasons: waiting-on-province: Province (MIT) refused council's request to lower the speed east of the city to 50 km/h; HTB instead raised the in-city zone to 60. (Jac Siemens); engineering-warrant: Staff/engineering researched the recommendation; follow it rather than extend the restriction. (Michael Zwaagstra); enforcement-not-design: The restriction only works if it is enforced. (Chris Goertzen)
vote: carried (amendment by Siemens defeated; counts not stated)
notes: Street names as transcribed: 'Craker' (Kroeker Ave), 'Goosen' (Goossen Ave). Speaker E, who said he could agree with the Siemens amendment, is not identified.

title: Albert Street residents ask for a sidewalk and traffic help as Stonebridge/Loewen traffic grows
summary: Oct 2016: a resident letter (T.M.) asked for a sidewalk on Albert Street, busier since the new primary health care centre and the Stonebridge Crossing extension; council asked staff for a cost report (moved by a councillor identified as Siemens, seconded by Zwaagstra). Jul 2017: at the 333 Loewen Blvd rezoning hearing, Albert Street residents again raised traffic and children's safety; staff said there were no immediate sidewalk plans and no traffic impact study had been required of the developer. Councillor Fehr floated a stop sign at Albert Street and Loewen Boulevard.
status_detail: Report requested Oct 4, 2016; by Jul 18, 2017 there were 'no immediate plans' for a sidewalk. No stop sign or traffic impact study requirement followed in the period. The rezoning got second reading (R17-141, Zwaagstra/S. Penner, unanimous).
reasons: study-first: Monitor and get the information first; established neighbourhoods use a 50/50 cost share with owners. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: Older neighbourhoods fall under the 50/50 local-improvement formula. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: T.M. (letter, Oct 2016) asked for a sidewalk. Jul 2017: G.C. (Albert Street) said traffic had increased 'tenfold' since Stonebridge opened; A.M. (Albert Street) said his children walk a very busy road to school and asked for a sidewalk. The applicant's representative (R.R.) said the project would generate less traffic than the former medical clinic but had not done a traffic study.
notes: The Oct 2016 cost report is not found in the period's transcripts.

title: Resident letters about PTH 52 West (2016) and a PTH 52 East paved shoulder (2017) taken as information
summary: Council received a resident letter (L.P.) about PTH 52 West on Oct 18, 2016 and an email (W.W.) asking for a paved shoulder on PTH 52 East on Nov 21, 2017. Both were taken as information without discussion.
status_detail: Received as information; no action or referral to the province recorded in the transcript.
reasons: provincial-highway: PTH 52 is a provincial highway; no reason was stated on the record. (council (implied))
public: L.P. (letter on PTH 52 West, content not read aloud); W.W. (email requesting a paved shoulder on PTH 52 East).
notes: Letter contents are in the agenda packages, not the transcripts; not checked.

title: 2016 traffic count: construction cut PTH 12 volumes; Loewen Blvd the hardest remaining intersection
themes: traffic-study; pth12; pth52; intersection; pedestrian; bypass
summary: The 2016 count showed construction-season drops on PTH 12 (Superstore intersection down about 30%, about 1,000 cars an hour) but long-run growth of 1–3% a year. Industrial Road at PTH 52 West exceeded its capacity (third year warranting signals); PTH 12 at Loewen Boulevard, with no dedicated east-west left-turn lanes, was the most challenging remaining intersection; a new 'pedestrian desire line' analysis suggested crossings at Millwork/Stonebridge and Friesen/Woodhaven. Council accepted the report and acted on it (see the two 2017 requests below).
status_detail: Report accepted (seconded by Funk; carried). Loewen Blvd/PTH 12 was flagged but no request for it was made in the period.
figures: Superstore/PTH 12 down ~30% (~1,000 cars/hour); 10-year traffic growth 1–3%/yr (transcript 0:03:28).
reasons: enforcement-not-design: No number of lights and crosswalks replaces careful drivers and enforcement. (Chris Goertzen)
notes: The same turn (B, 0:22:34) also credits MIT's 'smart lights' on PTH 12.

title: Council formally asks the province for signals at Industrial Road/PTH 52 and crosswalks on PTH 12
themes: pth52; pth12; signals; intersection; pedestrian; school-zone
summary: After three straight years of counts showing a signal warrant at Industrial Road and PTH 52 West, council made its first official request to the province for signals there, and by friendly amendment asked Manitoba Infrastructure for crosswalks near the school at Millwork/Stonebridge and at Friesen/Woodhaven (seniors' housing) on PTH 12. Staff had advised waiting for a three-year pattern. In Aug 2017 there was still no reply from the province.
status_detail: Signals: Manitoba Infrastructure gave the go-ahead (correspondence noted Mar 6, 2018) and lights were in place by Feb 2020. Crosswalks: on Mar 6, 2018 the city was still waiting for the PTH 12 crossing near Steinbach Christian School; no outcome found for Friesen/Woodhaven in the period.
figures: Third consecutive year the count showed a signal warrant (transcript 0:09:56–0:10:23).
reasons: study-first: Staff advised waiting until a definite pattern (three years of warrants) before asking. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); engineering-warrant: Raw pedestrian counts did not meet the formal crossing warrant; the new desire-line analysis only marks 'candidates'. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); provincial-highway: Signals on PTH 52 are the province's decision and 'will take quite some time'. (Chris Goertzen)
seconder: Councillor Penner (Susan or Cari; not determined)
notes: Follow-up evidence after the period: 2018-03-06 transcript 1:11:36 (mayor: the Minister of Infrastructure 'has given us the go-ahead'); 2020-02-18 transcript mentions 'the lights now at Industrial Road and 52'.

title: Council asks the Highway Traffic Board to review the PTH 52 West speed transition
summary: The mayor suggested asking the Highway Traffic Board to move the 80-to-50 km/h transition on PTH 52 West farther west, past Industrial Road, as a faster interim fix than signals. Zwaagstra asked what evidence beyond growth the city had; council first left it for 'another time', then later the same meeting a Councillor Penner moved the request (seconded by Funk) citing MPI collision data, and it carried.
status_detail: Request carried; no Highway Traffic Board decision was reported to council in the period.
figures: Speed 80 km/h until just past Lund Road; 50/80 transition at Loewen Windows (transcript 0:35:26–0:35:38).
reasons: provincial-highway: Speed limits are a Highway Traffic Board decision; signals are a Manitoba Infrastructure regional decision. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); study-first: Asked what evidence beyond traffic growth would support the request. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Councillor Penner (Susan or Cari; not determined)
notes: Councillors Fehr and one Councillor Penner were absent and excused on 2017-01-17, so the Penner present is one of the two; which is not stated.

title: Main Street crosswalk bands at Kroeker and Friesen repaired (partial tender, 50/50 with province)
summary: Tenders to replace the decorative crossing bands at the downtown Main Street intersections came in about $160,000 over the $360,000 budget, so council awarded only parts A, B and D ($311,590, Maple Leaf Construction) covering Kroeker and Friesen. The work is cost-shared 50/50 with the province because Main Street is a provincial highway; the rest was left for a future year.
status_detail: Partial award; remaining intersections depend on the provincial program being extended.
figures: Budget $360,000; full tender nearly $450,000; award $311,590 (transcript 0:10:02).
reasons: cost: Above budget the city would pay 100% rather than 50%, so stay within budget. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Pedestrian-safety maintenance rather than a capacity project; included because it is the main downtown crossing work in the period.

title: Siemens asks for a traffic count at Loewen Boulevard and Hespeler Avenue
summary: After being caught in two traffic jams, Siemens asked that the Loewen Blvd/Hespeler Ave intersection (outside the annual PTH count) be studied. By consensus council asked staff to add it to their informal in-house counts rather than the consultant's study.
status_detail: Staff count agreed by consensus; no result reported to council in the period.
reasons: cost: Use informal staff counts without the extra cost of adding it to the consultant study. (Chris Goertzen)

title: Stop sign added at Industrial Road and North Front Drive
summary: A business letter asked for a stop sign at Industrial Road and North Front Drive (by the Diner on 52) for safer access. Staff and the city engineer reviewed it in advance and recommended it, mirroring the Lund Road/North Front Drive configuration; council approved it.
status_detail: Approved; staff noted signals at Industrial/PTH 52 would trigger a review of all movements at that intersection.
public: Request came by letter on behalf of a business (Diner on 52).
notes: Chair (speaker A) is addressed as 'Mr. Deputy Mayor'; Funk, Zwaagstra, Siemens and both Penners are named separately, so the chair is most likely John Fehr (not stated).

title: No-parking zone extended on Reimer Avenue West at Harvest Drive after a resident request
summary: A resident (K.S.) asked for a longer no-parking zone on Reimer Avenue West near Harvest Drive. The city engineer found heavy traffic and on-street parking and recommended extending it to just west of the second leg of Cambridge Way; council approved.
status_detail: Approved; takes effect when signs are installed. Siemens flagged that parked cars may shift to side streets and said he would watch it.
public: K.S. (resident letter) requested the change.

title: Hanover School Division asks for a 4-way stop, crossing and lower school-zone speed near Barkman Ave and Fourth St
summary: After a young person was reportedly injured, Hanover School Division wrote again asking for a 4-way stop at Barkman Avenue and Fourth Street, a pedestrian crossing and a lower school-zone speed. Staff recalled the 2014 school-zone bylaw (Southwood, Stonybrook, Woodlawn) and that council had earlier kept the 2-way stop and changed parking instead. Council referred the letter to administration by consensus.
status_detail: After the period, council approved a 4-way stop at Barkman Avenue and Fourth Street on Jan 16, 2018 (R18-009, moved Siemens, seconded Zwaagstra, unanimous). No change to the school-zone speed was found.
reasons: study-first: Not an expert; refer to administration for a report before deciding. (Earl Funk); traffic-flow: Cautious about an all-day 30 km/h zone that would slow traffic through town. (John Fehr)
public: Hanover School Division (organization) letter; an injury to a young person was referred to but not detailed.
notes: Chair is 'Madam Deputy Mayor' (one of the two Penners; not stated).

title: 80 Brandt Street hearing: residents describe accidents and congestion at Brandt St, Woodhaven and PTH 12
summary: At the hearing on Envision's request to redesignate 80 Brandt Street commercial, neighbours described frequent collisions at Brandt Street and Woodhaven/Friesen, heavy truck traffic, long waits on PTH 12 and seniors crossing without a controlled crossing. Council denied the plan change (moved by Siemens) on land-use grounds; traffic was not addressed by any motion.
status_detail: No traffic action followed in the period; the Jan 2017 request to the province for a crossing at Friesen/Woodhaven was still the only step on this corner.
figures: Resident estimate: 1 mile takes at least 15 minutes, with 2–3 light cycles per intersection (transcript 0:12:37).
reasons: provincial-highway: The crossing problem is 'really a provincial problem'. (resident B.B.)
public: K.L. (Brandt Street) described frequent sirens for accidents at Brandt and Woodhaven and heavy truck traffic; A.P. (Autumnwood) said Brandt is near capacity and an alternate route is needed; B.B. said the Main-to-McKenzie stretch of Brandt has some of the city's highest accident rates and seniors lack a safe crossing; another resident asked for reduced speed zones, sidewalks and turning lanes. These are residents' claims, not verified collision data.
notes: Brandt Street is the PTH 12 corridor through the city; the transcript spells it 'Brant'/'Brand'.

title: Narrow, busy Henry Street by the hospital: letter taken as information, one-way idea floated
summary: A resident letter (M.P.) said Henry Street near the hospital is narrow and treacherous. Staff said it is a standard 29-foot street and widening would need extensive study; a Councillor Penner suggested it might one day become one-way. Council took it as information.
status_detail: Taken as information; widening deferred because of cost.
figures: 60-foot road allowance, 29-foot road surface (transcript 1:38:18).
reasons: cost: Widening the street would be costly. (Chris Goertzen)
public: M.P. (letter) described the street as uncomfortable and treacherous, especially in winter.

title: Loewen Blvd at PTH 12: land taken for future turn lanes and repeated requests that the province make it a priority
summary: Loewen Blvd at PTH 12 was the city's worst intersection in the 2017 and 2019 counts (level of service F, no turn lanes). In 2018 council used a commercial variance (Mar 20) and a road-widening by-law (By-law 2104, Aug 2018) to secure corner land for future turn lanes. In Feb 2020 it forwarded the 2019 count and again asked Manitoba Infrastructure to make the intersection a priority (R20-034).
status_detail: No provincial commitment was made in 2018–2020. The intersection was rebuilt years later, sharing costs with the province (contract May 2024, fully reopened Nov 2025, about $11.2M), as recorded in the 2022–2026 report.
figures: LOS F (counts 2017, 2019; minutes 2018-01-02, 2020-02-18); eastbound left-turn wait 559 s (~9.5 min) at p.m. peak (Zwaagstra citing report, 2020-02-18 0:42:12); close to 3,000 vehicles/hour at peak (Mayor Funk, 2020-02-18 0:47:21)
reasons: waiting-on-province: options worked out with Manitoba Infrastructure; improvements proceed when city and provincial funding is approved (Troy Warkentin); provincial-highway: the city's role is to gather evidence and press the province to add turn lanes on its highway (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: John Fehr (By-law 2104 1st & 2nd); Susan Penner (3rd); Michael Zwaagstra (R20-034)
seconder: Cari Penner (1st); Michael Zwaagstra (2nd); Jac Siemens (3rd; R20-034)
notes: Rebuild cost and dates are from the 2022–2026 report, not re-verified here.

title: Requests to the province for pedestrian crossings on PTH 12 (Millwork Dr/Stone Bridge Crossing and Friesen/Woodhaven)
summary: The 2017 count recommended a half signal at PTH 12 and Millwork Dr/Stone Bridge Crossing (near the Christian school and Bible college) and a pedestrian corridor at PTH 12 and Friesen/Woodhaven. Council asked staff to follow up with the province; a March 2018 letter said the province was still looking into it. The 2019 count (Feb 2020) recommended flashing beacons (RRFB) at those two PTH 12 crossings and at PTH 52/Lund Rd, and an overhead flashing beacon at PTH 52/Kroeker Ave.
status_detail: No provincial installation was reported to council in 2018–2020. In Feb 2024 council again asked the province for flashing crosswalk lights on Main and Brandt (2022–2026 report).
figures: Recommendations from WSP counts (minutes 2018-01-02 item 6.1(i); 2020-02-18 item (j))
reasons: provincial-highway: crossings on PTH 12 are the province's decision; the city forwards requests (Troy Warkentin)

title: Province approves $350,000 for signals at PTH 52 West and Industrial Road after four years of met warrants
summary: The city's traffic counts showed signal warrants met at PTH 52 West and Industrial Road for four straight years. In March 2018 the Minister of Infrastructure confirmed $350,000 to install signals in the 2018/19 construction program; council received the letter as information and welcomed it.
status_detail: Signals were operating by Feb 2020, when Councillor Siemens noted more turning traffic there and more drivers using Park Road to avoid Loewen Blvd.
figures: $350,000 provincial approval (minutes 2018-03-06 item 25); 120 warrant points vs 82 threshold, 4th consecutive year (minutes 2018-01-02)
reasons: waiting-on-province: a long-standing concern with numerous collisions; signals came only once the province approved them (Chris Goertzen)

title: 2017 traffic count accepted; staff told to work with the province on Loewen Blvd and on pedestrian crossings on PTH 12
themes: traffic-study; pth12; pth52; intersection; signals; pedestrian
summary: On Jan 2, 2018 the city manager presented WSP's 2017 Annual Traffic Count (18 intersections). It found Loewen Blvd at PTH 12 at level of service F with no turn lanes, signal warrants met at PTH 52 and Industrial Road for a fourth straight year, and recommended pedestrian crossing control at two PTH 12 intersections. Council's consensus was for staff to confer with Manitoba Infrastructure on Loewen Blvd and follow up on the two crossings.
status_detail: Report acknowledged and copies sent to Manitoba Infrastructure; follow-ups are tracked in the Loewen Blvd, PTH 52/Industrial signal and PTH 12 crossing items. No council discussion of a 2018 count was found in the 2019 minutes; the 2019 count came to council in Feb 2020.
figures: 18 intersections; PTH 12 p.m. peak volumes up about 1–3% a year over 10 years; Loewen/PTH 12 LOS F; PTH 52/Industrial Rd 120 warrant points vs 82 threshold, 4th consecutive year; Loewen/Hespeler St N acceptable, 'traffic control modifications are not warranted' (minutes 2018-01-02, items 6–6.5)
notes: No video/transcript exists for Jan 2, 2018; everything here is from the minutes.

title: 4-way stop at Barkman Ave and Fourth St approved against staff advice; school speed zone not added
summary: Hanover School Division asked (2015 and Oct 2017) for a review of the 2-way stop at Barkman Ave and Fourth St and of the speed zone on Barkman. Staff recommended keeping the 2-way stop and 50 km/h, adding a no-stopping zone for sight lines. Council instead amended Traffic By-law 1350 to make the intersection a 4-way stop (R18-009).
status_detail: 4-way stop approved; the reduced-speed school zone on Barkman was not adopted (staff recommended keeping 50 km/h).
reasons: engineering-warrant: staff review of school type, site layout and street configuration did not support a reduced-speed school zone (Troy Warkentin)
public: Hanover School Division (organization) made the request.
notes: No video/transcript for Jan 16, 2018; minutes only.

title: Earlier PTH 12 intersection program (built before 2018) cited as the model: four intersections, $7M, split 50/50 with the province
summary: In 2018–2019 council and staff repeatedly pointed to a multi-year program, finished by 2017, that rebuilt four major PTH 12 (Brandt St) intersections (including Park Road) with the province on a 50/50 basis. By the end of the 2014–2018 term the city counted 16 signalized intersections, eight added under Mayor Goertzen.
status_detail: Completed before this period; staff said in Feb 2020 that fixing the worst intersections left Loewen Blvd as 'a new worst one'.
figures: 4 major PTH 12 intersections, $7M, 50/50 city–province (Mayor Funk, 2019-10-01 0:00:05); 16 signal lights, 8 added 'on your watch' i.e. during Goertzen's years on council (Councillor Siemens, 2018-10-16 0:53:48); 4 sets of lights added 2010–2018 (Siemens, 2018-10-16 0:00:23)
notes: The program itself predates this period; included as context for the Loewen Blvd requests.

title: Cost-share request to replace pedestrian crossing bands on Main Street (PTH 52) turned down by the province
summary: Council voted to join Manitoba Infrastructure's Urban Highway Fund cost-share program to replace the uni-stone and concrete pedestrian crossing bands on Main Street at Elm Ave, William Ave and the Elmdale School corridor (R18-036). In August 2018 the province wrote that no funding was available.
status_detail: Province declined funding (letter received Aug 21, 2018); no further action recorded in this period.
reasons: waiting-on-province: the work depended on provincial cost-share funding, which was not provided (Troy Warkentin)

title: PTH 52 West speed zone: council asked for 50 km/h, the province set 70 km/h
summary: Council had asked the province to cut the speed limit on PTH 52 West to 50 km/h. At an Apr 17, 2018 Highway Traffic Board hearing attended by the city manager, the province's traffic engineer recommended 50 km/h only from PTH 12 to near Lund Road, 70 km/h from Lund Road to past Industrial Road, and 80 km/h to Keating Road. The board accepted that, and temporary 70 km/h signs were up by May 1, 2018.
status_detail: Speed lowered from 80 to 70 km/h rather than the 50 km/h council requested.
figures: 50/70/80/100 km/h zones (minutes 2018-04-17 item 7; transcript 0:05:08); temporary 70 km/h signs (minutes 2018-05-01 item 14)
reasons: provincial-highway: speed on PTH 52 is set by the province through the Highway Traffic Board, not the city (Troy Warkentin)
notes: The date of council's original 50 km/h resolution is before this period and was not checked.

title: Residents' traffic objections at infill rezoning hearings usually judged minor
summary: Neighbours raised traffic and congestion at many infill hearings (First Street 2018 and 2020, Maplewood 2018 and 2019, Stonebridge/Maplewood 2020, Ellis Ave 2020). Council members generally answered that the added trips were small and that the same objection could be made to any added density; staff said they knew of no traffic-loading complaints in neighbourhoods with more apartments. Outcomes were mixed and mostly turned on other factors.
status_detail: Approved, among others: First Street (R18-090, May 2018), Maplewood By-law 2120 (R19-147, Jul 2019), 78 First Street By-law 2148 (R20-127/128, Jun 2020). Denied: Maplewood By-law 2101 (R18-191, Aug 2018) and By-law 2152 (R20-156, Aug 2020); reasons for the denials were not reviewed here.
figures: 82 multifamily units approved on First Street in two years (city manager, 2020-06-16 0:31:47)
reasons: impact-small: a 10-unit building adds about 9–10 vehicles a day; traffic concerns apply to any added density (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Neighbours (initials not recorded here) cited through traffic, children's safety and difficulty turning onto PTH 12 or Giesbrecht St.
notes: Grouped item; the housing-development report covers these rezonings in detail.

title: Traffic kept as one of four RCMP priorities each year; provincial traffic unit based in Steinbach
summary: Each year council confirmed four RCMP community priorities, including 'Crime Reduction – Traffic' (R18-107 in 2018, R19-096 in 2019, and again in May 2020). In 2018 Councillor Siemens asked the staff sergeant about the stream of collisions on Brandt St/PTH 12. By 2019 a provincially funded RCMP traffic section of five members was working out of the Steinbach detachment, writing 25–30% of its tickets in the city at no cost to the city.
status_detail: Priorities confirmed in 2018, 2019 and 2020; the traffic section was in place from spring 2018.
figures: Traffic offences 567 (2016) to 744 (2017); impaired driving 62 to 44; 130 cellphone tickets in April 2018 (RCMP, 2018-05-15 0:04:51); 5-member traffic section, 25–30% of tickets in the city (RCMP, 2019-04-16 0:11:39, 0:19:33)
reasons: enforcement-not-design: enforcement described as the main response to collisions and speeding (RCMP Staff Sergeant (H.L.))
public: RCMP Staff Sergeant H.L. (delegation) reported on traffic enforcement.
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (2018); Jake Hiebert (2019); a Councillor Penner (2020)
notes: No minutes PDF for May 19, 2020 was found; the 2020 vote is from the transcript. The RCMP staff sergeant is a public servant appearing as a delegate and is identified by initials per the rules.

title: Clearspring Greens residents' safety push on Old Tom and Park Road: lights, lower speed and a pathway, with a split over who pays
summary: Clearspring Greens has no sidewalk link to the city; residents said paving Old Tom Road turned Old Tom, Park Road and Hespeler into a fast perimeter route around Main and PTH 12. After a 2018 letter (sent to a study session on Councillor Siemens' motion) and a July 2019 delegation of about 100 residents, council added streetlights at Old Tom/Park Rd (R19-033, Feb 2019), cut Old Tom's limit to 60 km/h (By-law 2123), and in Jan 2020 advanced a $625,000 pathway as a local improvement mostly paid by the 146 homes. Siemens and Jake Hiebert opposed the cost to residents and lost 2–5 on a cheaper version.
status_detail: After 78 objections council cancelled the 2020 plan (R21-011, Jan 2021), adopted a 50/50 cost split capped at $1,610 per lot without lighting (R21-012), and awarded construction in April 2021 (R21-077).
figures: $625,000 estimate, 3 m asphalt path with lighting and fencing, 146 benefiting properties (city manager, 2020-01-07 0:11:07); 2021 cap $1,610 per parcel (R21-012)
reasons: no-budget: the 2019 budget had no room for the pathway (Earl Funk); fairness-precedent: would not raise what other taxpayers pay for a path that mainly serves one neighbourhood (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: a connecting path for the homes paying for it, not part of a wider network (Damian Penner)
public: Residents (delegation led by M.F., July 16, 2019) said children cannot safely walk or bike on Old Tom Road; one resident (D.) called it a traffic problem caused by Old Tom becoming a perimeter road; another (N.L.) warned of a fatality (unproven claim about an earlier death near Timber Falls not checked). At the Jan 7, 2020 hearing most residents objected to the cost.
mover: Jake Hiebert (R19-033); Damian Penner (R20-005); Michael Zwaagstra (R20-012)
seconder: Bill Hiebert (R19-033); Michael Zwaagstra (R20-005); Damian Penner (R20-012)
vote: R20-005 5-2 (against: Siemens, J. Hiebert); R20-012 6-1 (against: Siemens)
notes: Mainly an active-transportation and local-improvement funding item; included because residents and members framed it as traffic safety on Old Tom/Park Road. Jan 2021 outcome from the motions CSV (outside this period).

title: Transportation plan put off during the 2018 community plan update; highway access plan waits for the province
summary: At the July 17, 2018 hearing on the new Official Community Plan, the city planner answered provincial planning comments on transportation: the city wants a transportation plan in future but not immediately, and the PTH 12/PTH 52 Highway Access Management and Transportation Plan would not be adopted by the city until Manitoba Infrastructure adopts it.
status_detail: No transportation master plan was adopted in 2018–2020; the 2022–2026 report finds none as of 2026.
reasons: waiting-on-province: highway access plan not adopted until the province adopts it (Lacey Gaudet); study-first: a transportation plan wanted 'within the future' but not immediately (Lacey Gaudet)
notes: Lacey Gaudet is named as the city planner in the Aug 7, 2018 transcript.

title: Resident's request for stop signs at Reimer Ave and Elmdale St referred for traffic data
summary: A resident (M.T.) wrote asking for stop signs on Reimer Ave at Elmdale St. Councillor Funk asked for the latest counts or a study; council's consensus was for administration to report on past traffic analysis and whether a count was warranted.
status_detail: Information was to go to council members' mail bins; no public result was found in later minutes.
reasons: study-first: wanted counts to see what is warranted before acting (Earl Funk)
public: M.T. (resident) requested stop signs along Reimer Ave at Elmdale St.

title: Questions about the new lane layout at McKenzie Ave and Brandt St (PTH 12)
summary: After the McKenzie Ave/PTH 12 intersection was widened in 2018, Councillor Zwaagstra relayed complaints that eastbound drivers going straight must use the right lane and then cut left. The city manager said the layout followed the consultants' analysis and the city's Highway Access and Transportation Plan, and offered to ask engineering for more detail. Councillor Fehr said similar layouts work for heavy trucks if lines are kept painted.
status_detail: Staff offered further information; no follow-up was recorded at a council meeting.
reasons: engineering-warrant: layout based on consultants' assessment of counts and turning movements and the access plan (Troy Warkentin)

title: Maximum Speed Limits By-law 2123 lowers limits on growing city roads (e.g., Old Tom Rd 70 to 60 km/h)
summary: Provincial changes in late 2018 gave municipalities authority over speed limits on their own roads (not PTH 12 or 52) and required a maximum speed limits by-law by Sept 1, 2019. Council passed By-law 2123, lowering limits on several roads, including Old Tom Road from 70 to 60 km/h and some annexed roads from 90 to 70 km/h.
status_detail: Adopted Aug 6, 2019 (R19-162). Limits on PTH 12 and 52 still need provincial approval.
figures: Old Tom Rd 70 to 60 km/h; some annexed roads 90 to 70 km/h (Zwaagstra, 2019-07-02 1:12:41; 2019-08-06 0:22:00)
reasons: provincial-highway: PTH 12 and 52 remain outside city speed jurisdiction (council (unidentified member))
seconder: Jake Hiebert (1st); Susan Penner (2nd); Bill Hiebert (3rd)
notes: The comment that PTH 12 and 52 remain provincial (2019-08-06 0:23:30–0:23:34) came from members the transcript does not identify.

title: Support for St. Pierre-Jolys' request to twin PTH 59 to PTH 52
summary: Council formally supported the Village of St. Pierre-Jolys' request that the province twin PTH 59 up to PTH 52, citing safety for all drivers (R19-268).
status_detail: Support given; the province's response was not tracked in council records for this period.
notes: Regional highway outside the city; no transcript for Dec 17, 2019.

title: Bush Farm Road traffic: road upgrades left to future development; mayor promises a plan for edge-of-city roads
summary: At a Mar 3, 2020 hearing on the next Parkhill phase, a Bush Farm Road resident (G.H.) objected that the gravel road carries heavy traffic from the southwest to the north end and asked when it would be upgraded. The city manager said road upgrades are triggered by development fronting the road, so none was required. Councillor (Susan) Penner asked for the issue at the July study session, and Mayor Funk said council needs a plan for how its edge-of-city roads will handle growth.
status_detail: The rezoning passed (R20-046/047); no plan for Bush Farm, Keating or Park Road West came to a council meeting in 2020.
reasons: development-first: developers build or upgrade the roads their development fronts; no fronting development, no upgrade (Troy Warkentin)
public: G.H. (resident, Bush Farm Road) objected to the secondary plan, rezoning and subdivision over the lack of a road plan; Southland Church traffic and Walmart-bound trips cited.
notes: Whether the July 2020 study session discussed Bush Farm Road was not checked (study sessions are not recorded).

title: 4-way stop at McKenzie Ave and Giesbrecht St not warranted; push-button pedestrian crossing approved instead
summary: A Meadows resident (M.K.) asked for a 4-way stop at McKenzie Ave and Giesbrecht St. In July 2020 Councillor Zwaagstra asked for a study and council agreed staff would count the intersection. In November engineering found traffic too light for a 4-way stop but enough pedestrians for an active crossing with push-button lights, markings and signs; council approved it on Councillor Siemens' motion.
status_detail: A pedestrian crossing was approved in place of the 4-way stop; installation was not verified. Siemens flagged speeding on McKenzie for the RCMP advisory committee.
reasons: engineering-warrant: traffic counts did not warrant a 4-way stop (Troy Warkentin); enforcement-not-design: speeding on McKenzie referred to the RCMP advisory committee (Jac Siemens)
public: M.K. (resident, Meadows subdivision) requested the 4-way stop.
notes: No minutes PDF for Nov 17, 2020 was found in downloads/minutes; decision from transcript. July 21, 2020 consensus is in the minutes (items 13–14).

title: New consolidated Traffic By-law 2164 keeps residents' right to request traffic control devices
summary: Staff presented a new traffic by-law consolidating Traffic By-law 1350 and others. At council's direction it keeps the public's right to ask council for traffic control devices, drops limits on vehicles on city property, and raises the disabled-parking fine from $100 to $250. Council gave first reading Nov 3, 2020 (R20-225).
status_detail: Second and third readings Jan 19, 2021 (R21-018, R21-019).
figures: Disabled-parking fine $100 to $250 (city manager, 2020-11-03 1:22:16)

title: Request for a 17th RCMP officer, with traffic enforcement among the reasons
summary: Council applied to the federal Minister of Public Safety for one more RCMP officer for 2021 (R20-243), the first increase since 2015. Councillor Zwaagstra, chair of the RCMP advisory committee, named traffic enforcement as a priority and said Steinbach has fewer officers per capita than comparable communities.
status_detail: Application approved by council; when the officer arrived was not verified (the 2022 budget funded an extra officer 'to deal with traffic issues', per the 2022–2026 report).
figures: 16 officers, about 1,000 residents per officer (Zwaagstra, 0:10:57); $160,000–180,000 per officer per year (city manager, 0:13:56)

title: Traffic By-law 2164 adopted, with higher fines for damaging traffic signs and misusing disability parking
summary: A rewritten traffic by-law (first reading Nov 3, 2020) came back for second and third readings. Councillor Zwaagstra highlighted the bigger fines: $1,000 for damaging or removing a traffic control device and up to $250 for parking in a disability space without a permit. A councillor added that ordinary penalties stay around $20–$40 and the by-law is not 'a tax grab'. Both readings passed unanimously.
status_detail: Second reading R21-018 (Zwaagstra/D. Penner) and third reading R21-019 (S. Penner/Siemens), both unanimous. The by-law was replaced in January 2025 by Traffic By-law 2254 (existing 2022–2026 report).
figures: Fine for damaging, defacing or removing a traffic control device $1,000; disability-parking permit offence raised from about $100 to $250 (Zwaagstra, 0:11:52); most other penalties in the $20–$40 range (unidentified councillor, 0:12:54).
public: None recorded.
notes: The 'not a tax grab' remark (Speaker E, 0:12:54) is not quoted because the speaker is not identified.

title: MPI speed display sign on Old Tom Road and Park Road, to be moved around the city
summary: Councillor Siemens said a new electronic speed sign on Old Tom Road and Park Road seemed to be slowing drivers and asked whether it worked. The city manager said Manitoba Public Insurance supplied the sign under an agreement with the city about November 2020, that MPI studies show drivers adjust when they see their speed, and that the city would move it around to areas with speeding complaints.
status_detail: The sign was in place; staff said results would be monitored and evaluated (minutes 14.1). No evaluation was reported to council in 2021–2022.
figures: One MPI-supplied sign, first placed about November 2020 (Warkentin, 0:29:23).
public: Staff cited one email from a driver who slowed down after seeing the sign.

title: Loewen Blvd / PTH 12 intersection rebuild: design contract and $3.5M borrowing approved, cost shared with the province
summary: Staff called Loewen Blvd at PTH 12 'the next most congested intersection in the city'. Council hired WSP to design the rebuild in July 2021 and passed a local improvement by-law in Dec 2021 – Mar 2022 to borrow $3.5M over five years, with the province paying most of the rest. The mayor said he had named it the city's top priority to the infrastructure minister in May 2019. A landowner on the corner asked for a third westbound lane and a median opening; the mayor said that hearing was only about the borrowing.
status_detail: WSP design contract (R21-150, Jul 20, 2021); By-law 2187 first and second readings Dec 7, 2021 (R21-250, R21-251), Municipal Board approval, third reading Mar 15, 2022 (R22-067), all unanimous; listed in the 2022 capital renewal program (minutes Apr 5, 2022). Construction planned for 2022–2023 was postponed: the $9.98M contract was awarded in May 2024 and the intersection reopened Nov 24, 2025 at about $11.2M in total, about $6.1M of it the city's (existing 2022–2026 report).
figures: Estimate $8.275M: borrowing $3.5M over 5 years (about $853,000 a year at up to 7%), grants and other funding $4.545M, city reserves $230,000; about $67.50 a year for a $200,000 home (Warkentin, 2021-12-07 0:19:21). WSP design and project administration $414,302 plus disbursements; 5 proposals (minutes R21-150). Province covers 'just over $4.5 million' (Zwaagstra, 2022-03-15 0:15:50).
reasons: provincial-highway: the province pays for the surface works; the city pays for the pipes underneath because they are city infrastructure (Jac Siemens); waiting-on-province: the city named it its priority to the minister in May 2019; provincial funding 'changed back and forth' before the deal (Earl Funk)
public: K.P., speaking for his family's corner property, said westbound traffic on Loewen has no north-turn lane, so drivers cut through Maplewood, Old Tom Road and his yard. He asked for three westbound lanes like McKenzie Ave and a median opening for his driveway. The mayor said the hearing was only about the borrowing and his comments would be looked at.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R21-150, R21-251, R22-067); Jac Siemens (R21-250)
seconder: Jake Hiebert (R21-150); Damian Penner (R21-250); Bill Hiebert (R21-251); Susan Penner (R22-067)
notes: The 2022–2023 construction schedule slipped to 2024–2025; the reasons for the delay were not discussed at 2022 meetings.

title: 2020 traffic count accepted and sent to the province: COVID cut PTH 12 traffic about 25%, Loewen Blvd still the worst corner
summary: The yearly WSP count of PTH 12 and PTH 52 intersections showed traffic down sharply in 2020 because of COVID. The city manager said not to base decisions on one year. Councillor Zwaagstra moved to accept it and send it to Manitoba Infrastructure, noting the 501-second average wait to turn left out of Loewen Blvd, a possible signal warrant at PTH 52/Giesbrecht and signal timing at PTH 12/Acres Drive. Councillor Jake Hiebert questioned the value of a pandemic-year count. Carried unanimously.
status_detail: Accepted and forwarded to Manitoba Infrastructure (R21-046, Zwaagstra/J. Hiebert, unanimous). Its Loewen Blvd and Giesbrecht recommendations were followed up (see 2021-loewen-pth12-intersection and 2022-giesbrecht-pth52-signals).
figures: 21 intersections on the two provincial highways, 3–6 p.m. on Oct 1, 2, 8 and 9, 2020 (minutes 11); PTH 12 volumes down about 25% from 2019 (Warkentin, 0:12:01); average wait for the eastbound left turn from Loewen Blvd 501 seconds (Zwaagstra citing the report, 0:16:28); fuel sales at a local co-op down as much as 42% (J. Hiebert, 0:18:33).
reasons: provincial-highway: the highways are provincial, so the city's role is to keep the province aware of its challenges (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: None recorded.

title: Signals requested at PTH 52 West and Giesbrecht Street after counts showed they were warranted
summary: The 2020 count first flagged a possible signal warrant at PTH 52 and Giesbrecht Street; the mayor said he had never thought of it until he read the report. The 2021 count, with three new PTH 52 West intersections, showed the warrant met for several years running. In February 2022 council forwarded the count and asked Manitoba Infrastructure to install signals in its 2023 capital program. Councillors described the near-impossible left turn onto the highway and growth on First Street and in Mitchell.
status_detail: R22-038 (Zwaagstra/D. Penner, unanimous) forwarded the 2021 count and requested signals for 2023. The province did not fund them in 2023; SteinbachOnline reported them operating on Oct 13, 2026, about four and a half years after the request.
figures: 2021 count: 24 intersections, three new on PTH 52 West, 3–6 p.m. on Oct 22, 28 and 29, 2021 (minutes Feb 15, 2022, item 18); 'all intersections counted for 24 years feature a positive growth rate' (Funk citing the report, 0:25:42).
reasons: provincial-highway: the city counts and asks; the province decides on and installs signals on PTH 52 (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Residents and businesses near the corner raised it again in Sept 2021 and Nov 2022 hearings (see 2021-first-street-traffic-study, 2022-6-first-street-giesbrecht).
notes: The province's 2023 deferral is reported from the existing 2022–2026 report (Mar 21, 2023 meeting), outside this period.

title: Street lights added on PTH 12 South (Brandt St) and PTH 12 North
summary: Council amended the Manitoba Hydro lighting contract to add 16 LED lights on PTH 12 South (Brandt Street) and later 12 on PTH 12 North. Councillor Siemens said people had asked for lights at the Madison Road left turn since the highway was four-laned 10–12 years earlier.
status_detail: R21-085 (Siemens/B. Hiebert, Apr 20) and R21-170 (J. Hiebert/Zwaagstra, Aug 3), both unanimous.
figures: 16 × 95 W LED on PTH 12 South, $3,079.68 a year; 12 × 240 W LED on PTH 12 North, $3,379.68 a year (minutes).
public: None recorded.

title: Church school in an industrial park refused, partly over truck and pedestrian traffic
summary: A church in the industrial park asked to rezone its site so it could run a school there. The majority refused. Councillor Damian Penner said industrial streets will carry more heavy traffic and have no paths or wide roads for children walking or cycling, and a permanent rezoning would leave future councils to add sidewalks.
status_detail: First reading of By-law 2170 defeated 2–5 (R21-090; for S. Penner, Siemens); motion to deny first reading carried 5–2 (R21-091, D. Penner/J. Hiebert).
reasons: traffic-safety: industrial park streets will carry heavy traffic and lack paths for children on foot or bike (Damian Penner); cost: if a school is allowed, sidewalks will be asked for in a few years (Earl Funk)
public: The applicant church wanted to run its own school in its existing building.
vote: 5-2 (against the school: Zwaagstra, B. Hiebert, D. Penner, J. Hiebert, Funk; for: S. Penner, Siemens)
notes: Mainly a land-use decision; included for its traffic-safety reasoning.

title: Zero front setback at 5 Loewen Blvd approved 6–1 over a councillor's sight-line worry near PTH 12
summary: An office building at 5 Loewen Blvd, just east of PTH 12, asked to build right up to the front property line. Councillor Jake Hiebert worried that drivers turning from PTH 12 onto Loewen, and drivers leaving the lot, would have their view blocked. Councillor Zwaagstra said professional staff had flagged no safety concern and he would go with their judgment. Approved 6–1.
status_detail: Variance V-2021-11 approved (R21-114, Zwaagstra/S. Penner), 6–1 with Jake Hiebert against.
figures: 0-ft front yard setback; about 20 ft from the lane to the building (Zwaagstra, 0:48:08).
reasons: engineering-warrant: staff are quick to flag safety concerns and flagged none here (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No written objections (minutes 6.2).

title: Traffic kept as one of the RCMP's four priorities for Steinbach (2021 and 2022)
summary: Each year council confirms the priorities it sets for the local RCMP detachment: police visibility, organized crime, property crime, and traffic. Council reconfirmed them in June 2021 and May 2022. In 2022 Councillor Zwaagstra reported that the new traffic officer had just started.
status_detail: R21-115 (Zwaagstra/D. Penner, Jun 1, 2021) and R22-119 (Zwaagstra/Siemens, May 17, 2022), both unanimous.
figures: 18 municipal RCMP officers after the traffic officer was added (Zwaagstra, 2022-05-17 0:18:40).
public: None recorded.
notes: Routine yearly item; grouped.

title: Calls for a traffic study before more First Street apartments; council adds 12 units without one (6–1)
summary: At first reading of a rezoning for 12 more units at 115 First Street, Councillor Siemens asked when a traffic impact study is required; staff said there is no set trigger and the plan only calls for one near a provincial highway. The mayor warned the street was 'getting more congested with every build'. At the hearing neighbours asked for a study. Siemens dropped his request so construction would not be delayed and pointed to the October count; Zwaagstra said 12 units add about 12 cars. Jake Hiebert moved to deny until a study was done (no seconder) and voted against.
status_detail: No traffic impact study was ordered. By-law 2182 passed second and third readings 6–1 (R21-187, R21-188; Jake Hiebert against). The October 2021 count led to the Feb 2022 request for signals at PTH 52/Giesbrecht (see 2022-giesbrecht-pth52-signals).
figures: 12 added units, about 12 cars (Zwaagstra, 0:32:47); 18 units already approved next door at 107 First Street; 2 registered objections (staff, 0:41:17).
reasons: no-policy-trigger: no set trigger; the plan only calls for a study near a provincial trunk highway (Troy Warkentin); minor-impact: 12 more cars is a very small fraction of First Street traffic (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: a study would delay construction and Brandt Street work skews counts; rely on the October count instead (Jac Siemens); minor-impact: drove First Street at 5 p.m. and it 'wasn't bad' (Bill Hiebert)
public: W.N. said neighbours' common concerns were traffic and parking and asked for a traffic study; S.C. (PTH 52 West) raised traffic and green space (minutes 6.5–6.6).
notes: The Sept 7 diarization mixes labels (E carries both Jake Hiebert and part of Siemens's remarks); only turns with a name cue right before are quoted.

title: Wyndham Estate Drive residents' speeding and construction-traffic complaints; last Hampton Village phase approved anyway
summary: At the hearing for the final 33-lot phase of Hampton Village, residents of Wyndham Estate Drive described speeding, drivers running the Ashford stop sign, heavy construction trucks and children walking to the bus with no sidewalks. One asked for a temporary construction road to Loewen Blvd. Even the developer's representative suggested a stop sign or speed bumps. Council approved the phase unanimously; Zwaagstra told residents to report stop-sign running to police, the mayor said a construction road would need a costly creek crossing, and staff said the streets meet national design guidelines.
status_detail: Rezoning By-law 2179 second reading (R21-176, Zwaagstra/D. Penner) and the subdivision (R21-177, J. Hiebert/B. Hiebert) carried unanimously; no construction access, stop sign or calming measure was ordered. Third reading followed a Municipal Board hearing (May 17, 2022, R22-129). A resident's 3-way stop request at Ashford came back in Aug 2022 (see 2022-wyndham-ashford-stop).
figures: 33 lots; 128 properties on one access versus a 120-lot policy guideline that staff said is about blockages, not traffic (staff, 0:42:04, 1:02:35).
reasons: development-first: won't stop completion of a long-planned neighbourhood because construction is disruptive (Michael Zwaagstra); police-decide: people running stop signs should be reported to police (Michael Zwaagstra); engineering-warrant: streets are designed to Transportation Association of Canada guidelines for the expected volume (Lacey Gaudet (City Planner)); cost: a temporary road to Loewen Blvd would cross a creek on land neither the city nor the developer controls (Earl Funk)
public: R.C., A.B., E.B. and K.R. (Wyndham Estate Drive and Preston Place) raised speeding, ignored stop signs, construction trucks and children's safety; R.C. said three calls to the city had changed nothing and proposed a construction road to Loewen Blvd. The developer's representative C.P. floated a stop sign at Ashford and Wyndham or speed bumps (minutes 11.5–11.14).
notes: Minutes spell the 0:56:17 speaker's name differently from the transcript; initials follow the minutes. Construction-traffic complaints on Home Street North the same month are recorded separately.

title: Construction trucks on residential streets (Home Street North): allowed for permitted projects
summary: Two letters from a Home Street North resident about traffic and construction vehicles were on the agenda. The mayor asked about policy; staff said trucks normally keep to designated truck routes but may use residential streets to reach a permitted work site for the life of the project. Council received the letters as information.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes 18); no change to truck rules.
reasons: development-first: temporary truck access to permitted construction is allowed for the life of the project (City administration)
public: C.B. wrote twice about traffic on Home Street North.
notes: The staff answer (Speaker F, 0:58:09) is not quoted because the label also carries a councillor in this file.

title: Province asked for authority to put red-light cameras on Main Street
summary: The second part of the street-racing motion asked the province for authority to install red-light cameras on Main Street, which would also catch speeders. Councillor Zwaagstra and the mayor both said they dislike the cameras in principle but wanted the option; only the province can allow them.
status_detail: Part of R21-195 (unanimous). No provincial reply and no later council discussion of cameras was found in meetings through 2026.
reasons: waiting-on-province: cameras need provincial permission; 'no guarantee of that' (Michael Zwaagstra); enforcement-not-design: prefers officers on the spot to cameras in principle (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Prompted by residents' street-racing letters (see 2021-traffic-officer-street-racing).
notes: Searched later transcripts for 'red light camera', 'photo radar' and 'camera': no follow-up found.

title: Street racing on Main Street: council adds an RCMP officer dedicated to traffic
summary: After letters, emails and calls about street racing on Main Street, Councillor Zwaagstra moved to ask for an 18th municipal RCMP officer, dedicated only to traffic, from January 2022. He said regular officers cannot sit on Main Street when other calls come in. Councillor Jake Hiebert, a former Steinbach staff sergeant, said he had asked council for a traffic officer about 14 years earlier. The cost (about $200,000 a year) drove most of the 2022 tax increase. By May 2022 the officer was working, vehicles were being impounded for racing and the mayor reported many tickets.
status_detail: R21-195 (Zwaagstra/Siemens, unanimous). Funded in the 2022 financial plan (mill rate up 0.4 to 14.1, minutes Apr 5, 2022). The officer started full time in May 2022 (Zwaagstra, 2022-05-17 0:18:40).
figures: About $200,000 a year (Zwaagstra, 1:00:47; Funk, 1:10:15). 17 officers before, 18 after (Zwaagstra, 2021-09-07 1:00:47; 2022-05-17 0:18:40). 2022 mill rate 14.1, up 0.4 'mainly' for the officer (Zwaagstra, 2022-05-03 0:04:56).
reasons: cost: about $200,000 a year would affect the budget, but the problem justified it (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Letters from B.U., S.M. and L.D. about street racing and noise were on the agenda (minutes 19–21); the mayor said many more emails, calls and visits to his store had come in.
notes: Siemens's remarks as seconder (Speaker J/D, 1:05:57–1:06:10) are not quoted: the labels split mid-turn and also carry the chair.

title: Drivers running the 3-way stop at Chrysler Gate and South Park near the high school
summary: At a hearing for a 4-storey apartment at 71 Chrysler Gate, a neighbour said school traffic turns the 3-way stop at Chrysler Gate and South Park into 'a racetrack' for 10 months a year, with drivers, including teachers, ignoring the stop signs. Councillor Zwaagstra said through traffic is the problem and proposed raising the intersection at the next RCMP advisory meeting, noting the coming traffic officer. The variance was approved.
status_detail: Referred informally to the RCMP advisory group; no result was reported to council.
reasons: police-decide: an enforcement matter for the RCMP advisory group and the new traffic officer (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: E.W. (Springwood Bay) described the intersection as 'a racetrack' and 'a drag strip' at school times and said Chrysler Gate residents put up 'slow down' signs every summer.

title: Woodhaven Avenue speeding complaint referred to the RCMP
summary: At a hearing for an apartment on Woodhaven Avenue, a neighbour described speeding late at night and activity in the park lot. The mayor said speeding is an RCMP matter, asked Councillor Zwaagstra to raise it with the staff sergeant, told her to call police when it happens, and said a dedicated traffic officer was coming that spring.
status_detail: Passed to the RCMP advisory group; no result reported to council.
reasons: police-decide: speeding and littering are RCMP issues; call when it is happening (Earl Funk)
public: N.P. (Whitby Crescent) described speeding on Woodhaven at night.

title: Weekday no-parking zone on Cottonwood Bend and Drive after complaints of loitering, 'squealing, racing'
summary: Neighbours of the walkway near the regional secondary school asked for no parking 8 a.m.–5 p.m. on weekdays, citing cars squealing and racing and students loitering. Council sent the letter to staff and the RCMP advisory group in May. In August, against administration's recommendation, council restricted parking at the neighbours' request, calling it a test.
status_detail: R22-182 (Siemens/Zwaagstra, unanimous): 'No Parking' Monday–Friday 8 a.m.–5 p.m. on Cottonwood Bend and Cottonwood Drive.
reasons: fairness-precedent: recommended against: not a through street and no parking problem (as reported by Siemens) (City administration)
public: A residents' letter (F.H.) and a signed petition from Cottonwood Bend and Cottonwood Drive asked for the restriction.
notes: Mainly about student loitering at a school walkway; included because the request cited racing and squealing tires.

title: Province asked for 'no engine brake' signs on all four highways into Steinbach
summary: Councillor Bill Hiebert said residents south of the city complained about engine-brake noise early and late. Staff said signs on provincial highways go through Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure and need a council resolution. Council passed one the same night, amended by Councillor Siemens to cover all four highway entrances.
status_detail: R22-177 (B. Hiebert/Siemens, unanimous) asked MTI for signs on PTH 12 North and South and PTH 52 East and West. No reply or installation was reported at later council meetings.
reasons: provincial-highway: signs on provincial highways go through MTI and require a council resolution (Adam Thiessen)
public: Residents south of the city (via Bill Hiebert and Siemens) complained of engine-brake noise.
notes: Later transcripts were searched for 'engine brake', 'engine retarder' and 'Jake brake': no follow-up found.

title: 3-way stop requested at Wyndham Estate Drive and Ashford Lane: sent to staff, later refused
summary: A Hampton Village resident who led the neighbourhood play-structure project asked for a 3-way stop at Wyndham Estate Drive and Ashford Lane, citing speed and many children. Councillor Susan Penner asked staff to study it once the play structure was in and school was in session. Councillor Damian Penner noted a past 4-way stop request at McKenzie and Giesbrecht had ended in a pedestrian corridor instead. Referred by consensus.
status_detail: Staff counted the corner on May 26, 2023 and found low volumes, speeds within the 50 km/h limit and waits under 15 seconds. On Jun 20, 2023 council refused the stop sign and instead created a 'no stopping' zone on Wyndham on both sides of Ashford (R23-125, 6–1, Susan Penner against).
reasons: engineering-warrant: study the corner when the play structure is in and school is in session (Susan Penner); engineering-warrant: the right answer may be a pedestrian corridor rather than a stop (Damian Penner)
public: K.S. (Hampton Village) asked for the 3-way stop because of speed and many children near a school and park.
notes: The 2023 result is from the Jun 20, 2023 minutes (outside this period).

title: Old Tom Road / Loewen Blvd neighbourhood approved as residents ask for a traffic study and an intersection plan
themes: residents; traffic-study; intersection; roundabout; transportation-plan; speed
summary: At the hearing for a 95-parcel neighbourhood at Old Tom Road and Loewen Blvd, residents asked what was planned for the Hespeler/Loewen and Old Tom/Loewen intersections, whether the 70 km/h limit would drop, and whether any traffic study had been done; one said Old Tom and Park Road are already used as 'a city bypass and speedway'. The mayor said stop signs or a traffic circle were under discussion and roads follow development. Councillor Siemens called the city's traffic 'horrendous' but said there was 'not a definitive plan'. Council approved the development unanimously.
status_detail: OCP By-law 2211, rezonings 2212 and 2213 (second reading) and the subdivision (R22-205, D. Penner/Siemens) carried unanimously; no traffic impact study was required. Council said the intersections would be discussed at long-term planning sessions. In April 2024 a 3-way stop at Loewen and Hespeler was defeated 3–4 and the mayor's preferred roundabout was not budgeted (existing 2022–2026 report).
figures: 95 parcels (30 RSF, 60 RLD, 4 RHD, 1 C-MX) (Warkentin, 1:23:35); Loewen Blvd posted at 70 km/h (J.C., 0:22:44).
reasons: development-first: let the development happen, then work on the road system (Earl Funk); study-first: traffic is part of long-term planning sessions, but there is no definitive plan yet (Jac Siemens); annual-count-instead: the city already counts traffic every October (Earl Funk)
public: J.C. asked about the Hespeler/Loewen and Old Tom/Loewen intersections and the 70 km/h limit; D.E. (Loewen Blvd since 1973) asked for a traffic count outside construction, saying he can hardly leave his driveway at rush hour; R.F. asked whether a vehicle and active-transportation study had been done and said a study should come first.
notes: The Hiebert who spoke at 1:20:40 about studying traffic at a planning session cannot be identified (map: low) and is not quoted.

title: Apartments beside PTH 52 and Giesbrecht advanced 5–2 over traffic objections, on the expectation that signals come first
summary: A 22–24-unit building at 6 First Street, on the PTH 52 corner, drew objections from Loewen Windows, whose staff use the intersection, that traffic already backs up on the highway and Giesbrecht. Councillor Damian Penner said the signals council had requested would be up well before the building was finished, and traffic could be analysed then. Councillor Siemens wanted a 30-ft highway buffer and called the corner one of the city's critical intersections. Second readings passed 5–2.
status_detail: The objection was not upheld: By-laws 2216 and 2215 passed second reading 5–2 (R22-251, R22-252; Siemens and Jake Hiebert against); third readings came Jul 4, 2023. SteinbachOnline reported the Giesbrecht signals operating on Oct 13, 2026.
figures: 22–24 units, 3 storeys; side yard toward PTH 52 moved from 5 to 8 ft (applicant, 0:33:00).
reasons: waiting-on-province: signals are already requested; analyse traffic once they are in (Damian Penner)
public: J.S. for Loewen Windows said traffic is frequently backed up on the highway and Giesbrecht, with heavy pedestrian traffic, and opposed the rezoning.
notes: Siemens's main stated reason was the highway setback and the building's look; traffic was a secondary point.

title: Neighbours' request for a traffic study at the McKenzie Avenue school crosswalk refused; fourplex advanced 5–2
summary: Neighbours objecting to a fourplex at 205 McKenzie Avenue, across from the regional secondary school, asked council to delay 60–90 days and have the city do a traffic impact study covering the walkway and signalled crosswalk on McKenzie. A mother described children crossing at 8–9 a.m. The majority said four units add only a few cars to a street already carrying school traffic. Siemens and the mayor voted against, calling it an extremely busy area.
status_detail: No traffic study was ordered; By-law 2217 passed second reading 5–2 (R22-253; Siemens and Funk against). A Municipal Board hearing followed in 2023; third reading passed Jun 18, 2024.
figures: 4 units, 7 parking stalls (applicant/residents); a student body of about 1,800 across the street (D. Penner, 1:21:22).
reasons: minor-impact: one home to four is minor; McKenzie traffic is mostly through traffic (Michael Zwaagstra); minor-impact: 3–4 more cars beside a school of 1,800 will not stress the street (Damian Penner)
public: C.K. (Cottonwood Bend), speaking for neighbours, asked for a delay and a traffic impact study including the pedestrian walkway and signalled crosswalk; V.H. (McKenzie Ave) worried about children's safety.

title: Request for overnight flashing signals on PTH 12 runs into provincial policy
summary: Councillor Siemens suggested PTH 12 signals flash overnight (about 11 pm to 5-6 am) and Councillor Susan Penner asked whether lights could be switched off at non-peak times. The city manager reported that MTI policy does not allow flashing yellows at signalized intersections on provincial trunk highways, but that an exception for urban Steinbach had been requested.
status_detail: Exception requested from MTI (reported Mar 21, 2023); no answer was reported to council in 2023-2024.
reasons: provincial-highway: MTI policy forbids flashing yellows at signalized intersections on PTHs as a safety protocol. (Troy Warkentin)

title: PTH 12 signal timing fixed after council asked staff to press the province
summary: On Jan 3, 2023 Councillor Siemens relayed complaints about badly timed signals and short left-turn phases on PTH 12 (Brandt St); Councillor Zwaagstra agreed and council, by consensus, sent administration to meet Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure (MTI). On May 2 the city manager reported that MTI had found several signals locked into the wrong cycles and corrected them in late April 2023.
status_detail: MTI reprogrammed the PTH 12 signals by the last week of April 2023; councillors reported improvement. Older camera-detection equipment was flagged for replacement with no date; the left turn at Penfield/Acres was still raised as a concern.
figures: Zwaagstra: almost 25 minutes from the Meadows to Clearspring Mall in December 2022 (transcript 0:22:57); 6 cars per left-turn cycle at Superstore/Co-op vs 10+ queued (Siemens, 0:19:46).
reasons: provincial-highway: Signals on PTH 12 are MTI's; the city can only request reviews, and MTI reviews mostly respond to complaints. (Troy Warkentin)
public: Residents' complaints relayed by councillors; no delegation.
notes: The planned follow-up SPC meeting with MTI was not found in the public record.

title: City joins Community Safety Officer program to weigh heavy trucks
summary: Council agreed to a self-funded Community Safety Officer Program agreement with the province and the RCMP so the city can stop and weigh heavy vehicles to enforce road weight restrictions under Traffic By-law 2164.
status_detail: Agreement authorized (R23-036). How often it has been used was not reported to council in 2023-2024.
notes: No transcript of the Feb 21, 2023 meeting exists; taken from minutes. Bill Hiebert was excused.

title: 2022 traffic count accepted and sent to the province
summary: Council accepted the WSP 2022 Steinbach Annual Traffic Count Program (21 intersections on PTH 12/Brandt and PTH 52/Main, counted on four October weekdays, 3-6 pm) and asked Manitoba Infrastructure to review its recommendations: signals at PTH 52 West and Giesbrecht St, and retiming at PTH 12 and Park Road. Councillors used the item to press PTH 12 left-turn problems.
status_detail: Report forwarded to MTI (R23-056). Giesbrecht signals deferred by MTI to 2024 (see 2023-giesbrecht-signals); signal retiming coincided with the separate PTH 12 review.
figures: PTH 12 at Park Road West 3,620 vehicles/hour (transcript 0:31:26); Giesbrecht St highest unsignalized intersection, 1,865 vph (transcript); PTH 52/Main volumes about 3% below 2019; PTH 12 volumes slightly above 2019 (transcript). Giesbrecht signals would improve northbound LOS F to B; Park Road retiming cuts overall delay 14 s (minutes Mar 21, 2023 item 11).
reasons: provincial-highway: Counts are forwarded to MTI, which decides on signals and timing. (Troy Warkentin)
notes: The transcript has the mayor naming 'Councillor Hebert' as seconder; minutes record J. Hiebert.

title: Signals at PTH 52 West and Giesbrecht St promised for 2024, not installed that year
summary: Signals at PTH 52 West (Main St) and Giesbrecht St had been warranted since the 2021 count and requested by council in 2021-2022. In March 2023 MTI said there was no budget for 2023 but it was scheduled for 2024; the 2023 count (March 2024) again said the work should be done in the 2024 construction season. No installation was reported by the end of 2024.
status_detail: Not built in 2024. (Later, outside this period: SteinbachOnline reported the signals operating on Oct 13, 2026.)
figures: Northbound LOS F at Giesbrecht in the PM peak (minutes Mar 21, 2023); 1,865 vph (transcript 0:31:26).
reasons: waiting-on-province: MTI had no budget funding to build it in 2023 and rescheduled it to 2024. (Troy Warkentin); provincial-highway: Highway signals are provincial; the city's role is data and lobbying. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Park Road West extension paved to Industrial Rd as a second route north
summary: Council awarded the Park Road West extension to Industrial Road to Friesen Hauling for $1,970,097, paid from reserves and timed with developer work, so the whole road would be concrete. Councillors presented it as an alternate route north during the coming Loewen Blvd/PTH 12 rebuild.
status_detail: Built in 2022-2023; city manager expected reopening after Oct 13, 2023.
figures: $1,970,097 + taxes, low of 5 bids (minutes R23-057).

title: $9.98M contract awarded to rebuild Loewen Blvd and PTH 12
summary: After years of postponement since the 2021 cost-sharing announcement, council awarded the Loewen Blvd and PTH 12 intersection renewal to Maple Leaf Construction for $9,981,284 (low of two bids). The city led the project under a funding agreement with MTI; the province covers highway components and signals, the city its underground utilities.
status_detail: Awarded (R24-107); construction 2024-2025. (Outside this period: fully reopened Nov 24, 2025, total about $11.2M, per the existing report.)
figures: Contract $9,981,284 + taxes (minutes R24-107); budget just under $10.4M with about $4.5M provincial (Warkentin, 0:19:35); Siemens put the city's cost at about $5.8M and the province's at about $4M plus hydro and signals (0:23:00); 2024 financial plan lists it in a $16.5M capital renewal program (minutes Apr 2, 2024).
reasons: waiting-on-province: Scope changes after the 2021 agreement forced repeated postponement. (Earl Funk)
notes: Figures differ by speaker (city $5.8M vs budget split $10.4M/$4.5M); both are as stated in the transcript.

title: Traffic stays a policing priority; dedicated traffic officer credited with less street racing
summary: In 2023 and 2024 council approved RCMP policing priorities that include traffic, and kept funding the dedicated municipal traffic officer added in 2022. The RCMP reported racing charges on Main Street; by April 2024 councillors said racing complaints had dropped, though collisions rose from 2022 to 2023. Councillor Jake Hiebert floated a second traffic officer paid by MPI.
status_detail: Priorities approved both years (R23-079, R24-075); traffic officer continued. No second officer was approved in 2023-2024.
figures: Racing fines of $672 each, 7-day suspensions and impoundment (RCMP, May 2, 2023); 5 provincial traffic members returned to the southeast (minutes May 2, 2023 item 6.3); collisions and impaired infractions up 2022-2023 (minutes Apr 2, 2024 item 11.1).
reasons: enforcement-not-design: Treats racing and speeding as enforcement problems: report them, ticket them, no warnings. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: A second traffic officer should be paid by MPI rather than the city. (Jake Hiebert)
notes: On Apr 2, 2024 the speaker map merges the Staff Sergeant with letter D (Damian Penner); his statements are not quoted.

title: Subdivision on Brandt St (PTH 12) refused, partly over a new highway driveway
summary: Council denied a subdivision at 68 Brandt Street creating a 31.5-foot lot, as administration recommended. Reasons were mainly infill compatibility, but Councillors Siemens and Jake Hiebert also cited that the province had not approved another driveway onto the four-lane highway.
status_detail: Application denied (R23-114). Status refers to the applicants' request.
reasons: provincial-highway: Highways had not approved a driveway; earlier lots there share driveways. (Jac Siemens)
public: Applicants G.L. and R.L.
notes: Minor item for this topic; mostly a land-use decision.

title: 3-way stop at Wyndham Estate Dr and Ashford Lane refused; no-stopping zone instead
summary: A Hampton Village resident asked in March 2022 for a 3-way stop at Wyndham Estate Drive and Ashford Lane, near a middle school and a new park. A staff review (May 26, 2023) found low volumes, speeds within 50 km/h, good visibility and waits under 15 seconds, so administration recommended no new stop sign. Council agreed 6-1 and added a no-stopping zone on both sides of Ashford Lane; Councillor Susan Penner voted against.
status_detail: No stop sign; no-stopping zone established (R23-125). The mayor suggested looking again the next spring once the park was in use; no return to council was found in 2024.
figures: Monitored 1 hour AM and 1 hour PM on school days (transcript 0:28:10); waits under 15 s per vehicle (0:25:17).
reasons: engineering-warrant: City's traffic-control guideline, reviewed every 5 years, does not support a stop sign. (Jac Siemens); engineering-warrant: Administration found the stop sign not warranted. (Jake Hiebert)
public: Request from a resident of 46 Wyndham Estate Drive (first heard Aug 2, 2022). Councillor Jake Hiebert credited a resident (K.S.) who had pushed for the stop and the park.
